title: Borrowing Chink Martin's tuba for a Wild West show job
summary: Laine's tuba player falls sick before a Wild West show job, so he borrows Chink Martin's tuba and hands it to a young player, who goes on to become a fine tuba man.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yes. Well, this is a coincidence that happened to me. I had a man, young man, playing tuba. His name was Joe Cascaro. And one day he took seriously sick. Now that evening he sent me word that he wasn't able to come down to play music with me and play us at this Wild West showcase. Well here I wasn't a terrible fix. Well a friend of mine, I thought of the Chinaman, Martin. I runs up to Casco and I borrow his tuba. And I give the tuba to this boy to play. He said to me, I don't know nothing about... I said you shove that in your face and play it. That's all. I don't know nothing about tuba. So we played them jobs. We finished that contract. I finished that contract. And it was a fellow by the name of O'Brien, young Buffalo Bill. Young Buffalo Bill. Young Buffalo Bill. Yes, he had that show. So we played, went down the corner, we played, went back to the lot.
This was a marching band? Marching band? Marching band. Marching band.

Marching band. He said he was a champion. I'll tell you that's right. But I'll be there. He pumped on that tuba remarkably. And I took notice to it. And I said to him, say, boy, I said, why don't you get yourself a good tuba? He said, I believe I will. So I think he went and got one of them hurricanes. They were like a bretter, you know, you put over your head. Yeah. It was a double-E flat. A double-B flat, that's what it was. So he went and got one of them. I think he bought a second-handed. And he said, I'm going to play tuba from now on. I said, I wish you would. He said, I can put my hand on you at any minute. I won't have to run around for the jet fellas. So sure enough, he did. He learnt that tuba. And I mean, he turned out to be wonderful. Wonderful. Wonderful. What was his full name, Papa?

Martin Abraham. Martin Abraham. Yeah. Well, we call him Chink Martin. Chink Martin? Yeah. Yeah. Uh, Papa, let's get everybody's name down here. What's your name? Bill Stuckey. And your name? My name. Yeah, don't you know your name? Oh, yeah. That's what it is. You're Mrs. Lane, huh? Mrs. Lane, yeah. Mrs. Blanche Lane, huh? Yeah. And I'm Dick Allen. You want to hear it back now, Papa? Well, I'd like to. I'll see how it's found. All right. What did you think of that, Papa? Pretty good. Pretty good, huh? Papa, can I ask you a question or two? Can I ask you a question or two? Most anything in the world. All right, sir. I believe you said you were 91 years old. That's right. Do you know of any of the old musicians that are still living who are older than you are? No, not a one. As far as you know, you're about the oldest one. Not a one, but I know. Mm-hmm. What about the straight men? What about the straight men? Are there any of them living? The guys that played the straight stuff.
